candidates.title: Empirical evaluation of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) loops integrated with deterministic network verifiers across vendor-specific CLIs
candidates.research_question: How effective is a GVR pipeline (LLM generation + Batfish/VeriFlow-style verification + automated repair) at producing syntactically and semantically correct configurations across heterogeneous vendor CLIs and realistic failure perturbations?
hypotheses: A GVR pipeline will significantly reduce unsafe configuration deployments (measured by verifier-detected semantic violations and simulated rollback events) compared to LLM-only generation.
candidates.proposed_design: Construct a sandboxed emulation testbed with representative vendor CLIs (e.g., Cisco IOS, Juniper JunOS syntactic variants) using publicly available device images or emulators. Define a task bank of intent-to-configuration prompts (N≈200) including benign, malformed, and adversarial-intent prompts. For each prompt: (1) obtain LLM-generated configuration; (2) run deterministic verifier (Batfish/VeriFlow equivalent) to detect violations; (3) if violations found, invoke automated repair loop up to K=3 iterations; (4) simulate application in emulator and record execution trace and rollback behavior under injectable faults. Preserve full provenance and hashes.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task artifacts: prompt, generated config versions, verifier reports (violations, coverage), repair iterations, emulator execution logs (success/failure, induced outage), rollback attempts and outcomes. Aggregate counts of initial failures, repaired-success, repaired-failure, and unverifiable cases.
candidates.primary_outcome: Proportion of tasks resulting in successful, verifier-approved configuration that also execute without simulated semantic failure (simulated-runtime success rate) under heterogeneous vendor CLIs.
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute per-task paired comparison between LLM-only (first output) and final GVR output: difference in verifier pass rate and simulated-runtime success. Use McNemar’s test for paired binary outcomes (verifier pass; runtime success). Estimate 95% Wilson CIs for proportions. Stratify by vendor and adversarial vs benign prompts; perform logistic regression to identify predictors of repair success (features: vendor, prompt-adversarial flag, initial syntactic error count). Report provenance and failure-mode taxonomy.
risks: Deterministic verifiers may yield false negatives (miss semantic violations) causing overestimation of safety
Emulator/device-image limitations may not fully capture vendor runtime semantics
Automated repairs could introduce new, undetected semantic errors
Adversarial prompts could cause model outputs that break emulators or require manual intervention

candidates.title: Operational cost-latency tradeoffs of mixed verification policies for LLM-generated NetOps artifacts
candidates.research_question: Under operational latency constraints, how do mixed verification policies (fast lightweight verifier vs. slow full verifier, with optional abstention) affect false-acceptance, false-rejection, end-to-end latency, and cost for LLM-generated configurations?
hypotheses: A cost-aware mixed verification policy that uses a fast validator first and escalates to a full verifier only when uncertainty exceeds a threshold will achieve lower median latency for accepted changes with comparable false-acceptance rate to always-using full verification at lower average cost.
candidates.proposed_design: Simulate a NetOps pipeline with a task bank (N≈500) and two verifier tiers: lightweight (fast syntactic + schema checks) and heavyweight (full semantic model like Batfish). Instrument LLM generation uncertainty estimates (e.g., log-prob drift or calibrated confidence). Define policies: (A) full-verifier always, (B) light-only, (C) mixed-threshold with abstain/escalate. For each task, record verification decisions, latency, monetary-cost proxy, and whether runtime simulation (sandbox) shows semantic failure. Run multiple threshold sweeps to characterize Pareto frontier under latency budgets.
candidates.expected_data: Per-policy distributions: verification latency, total pipeline cost, verifier pass/fail counts, simulated-runtime failures, abstention rates; ROC-like curves of false-acceptance vs latency/cost.
candidates.primary_outcome: Tradeoff curve (latency vs false-acceptance rate) and policy Pareto frontier; quantify cost reduction at fixed false-acceptance target.
candidates.analysis_outline: Estimate median and 95% quantiles of latency and cost per policy. Use bootstrapped CIs for false-acceptance rates. Compare policies using paired comparisons across tasks; compute area under latency-vs-falseaccept curve. Perform sensitivity analysis across model uncertainty calibration and task difficulty strata. Report threshold values achieving specified operational budgets.
risks: Uncertainty estimates from LLMs may be poorly calibrated, invalidating threshold policies
Cost proxies may not map linearly to real economic costs in production
Simulated verifier performance (latency/throughput) may differ from production services under load

candidates.title: Adversarial-prompt and backdoor robustness of LLM-driven NetOps pipelines with verifier defenses
candidates.research_question: How susceptible are LLM-based NetOps pipelines (with standard verifier defenses) to adversarial prompts and implanted backdoor patterns that cause unsafe configuration outputs, and how effectively can verifier-based detection and repair mitigate such attacks?
hypotheses: Verifier-based defenses will detect a majority of naive adversarial prompts that induce syntactic/semantic violations, but carefully crafted backdoor-style prompt patterns can evade detection and lead to unsafe simulated runtime outcomes at a non-negligible rate.
Automated repair mechanisms will reduce but not eliminate successful backdoor-induced unsafe deployments.
candidates.proposed_design: Design adversarial prompt classes: (1) prompt-injection that subtly changes intent, (2) backdoor trigger phrases embedded in benign-looking prompts, and (3) distribution-shift prompts. Use an LLM to generate configs for a curated task set (N≈300) under attack and control. Apply verifier detection/repair pipeline identical to Candidate 1. Measure attack success rate (unsafe runtime despite verifier) and attacker stealth (verifier pass rate despite malicious intent). Evaluate detection enhancement strategies (pattern detection, prompt-sanitization) as mitigations.
candidates.expected_data: Per-attack-class metrics: generated config artifacts, verifier reports, repair iterations, emulator runtime safety outcomes, detection/stealth rates, mitigation effectiveness metrics.
candidates.primary_outcome: Attack success rate after verifier+repair (fraction of malicious inputs resulting in unsafe simulated runtime under verifier-approved deployment).
candidates.analysis_outline: Compute attack success proportions per class with 95% CIs. Compare success rates between baseline verifier and enhanced-mitigation pipelines using Fisher’s exact test. Model factors associated with successful evasion via logistic regression (features: attack class, trigger complexity, prompt length). Provide qualitative taxonomy of successful evasion patterns.
risks: Creating realistic backdoor triggers may require many model queries and risk unintentional propagation if artifacts are misused
Ethical concerns around publishing vulnerable prompt patterns (will contain disclosure controls)
Simulated runtime may under- or over-estimate real-world exploit impact

candidates.title: Design and validation of canary- and rollback-aware scoring metrics to predict operational risk of agentic NetOps actions
candidates.research_question: Can a composite scoring metric (combining verifier coverage, canary deployment simulation success, rollback-success probability, and abstention utility) predict actual operational risk (simulated outage probability) better than single-factor metrics?
hypotheses: A composite canary-rollback score will show stronger correlation with simulated runtime safety (lower outage probability) than any single metric (e.g., verifier pass rate) across diverse tasks and vendors.
Thresholding on the composite score will yield more practical operating points (higher true-negative rate for risky changes) for canary deployments than verifier pass/fail alone.
candidates.proposed_design: Define candidate submetrics: verifier-coverage fraction, canary-simulation pass rate (small-scale emulation), rollback-success rate under injected faults, LLM-confidence signal, and abstention rate. Compute composite score via weighted sum; learn weights on a training subset (Ntrain≈300) and test predictive performance on held-out tasks (Ntest≈200). For each candidate config, run canary simulation and full simulation to label actual runtime risk. Evaluate ROC/AUPRC of composite vs single metrics.
candidates.expected_data: Per-config submetric values, composite scores, binary labels (simulated outage/no outage), canary vs full outcomes, confusion matrices, ROC and calibration plots.
candidates.primary_outcome: Predictive performance (AUC-ROC and AUPRC) of composite score vs best individual metric for predicting simulated outage on held-out tasks.
candidates.analysis_outline: Train composite scoring weights with logistic regression (regularized) on training set; evaluate AUC-ROC and AUPRC with bootstrapped CIs on test set. Compare AUCs using DeLong’s test. Report calibration (Brier score) and decision-curve analysis for operational thresholds. Perform ablation studies removing each submetric.
risks: Learned weights may overfit to synthetic task bank and not generalize to production distributions
Canary simulation fidelity limits external validity
Operational thresholds may be context-specific and require per-organization tuning

candidates.title: Evaluating robustness of agentic tool-selection to deceptive tool descriptions in NetOps tool registries
candidates.research_question: How robust are LLM-based agent tool-selection mechanisms to deceptive or marketing-biased tool descriptions, and can lightweight registry-validation checks reduce selection of unsuitable tools?
hypotheses: Agents relying on textual tool descriptions will select suboptimal or unsafe tools at a non-trivial rate when registry descriptions are deceptive, increasing downstream failure rate; adding structured capability metadata and registry validation checks will reduce unsafe tool selection.
A small set of automated registry-validation heuristics (schema checks, capability tests) will significantly decrease downstream failure rates with modest additional registry-maintenance cost.
candidates.proposed_design: Simulate a tool registry with Ntools≈50 entries, some intentionally given deceptive descriptions (overclaims, missing constraints). Implement an LLM-based agent that selects tools based on descriptions to accomplish NetOps tasks (N≈200). Compare agent performance under: (A) raw registry, (B) registry with structured metadata enforced, (C) registry with metadata plus runtime capability probes (lightweight validation). Measure tool-selection mismatch rate and downstream configuration/runtime failure rate.
candidates.expected_data: Per-task records: selected tool, description text, structured metadata, registry-validation flags, downstream verifier/ emulator failure outcomes, selection mismatch counts, and probe results.
candidates.primary_outcome: Reduction in downstream failure rate attributable to registry validation (difference in failure proportion between raw registry and validated registry conditions).
candidates.analysis_outline: Compare proportions of tool-selection mismatch and downstream failures across conditions using paired tests (McNemar). Model predictors of misselection via multinomial logistic regression (features: deception-type, tool-category, prompt ambiguity). Report cost/benefit estimate of registry validation (effort vs reduction in failures).
risks: Constructed deceptive descriptions may not fully capture real-world marketplace tactics
Runtime probes may have false negatives/positives, leading to incorrect registry flags
Ethical considerations in publishing deceptive-description templates; mitigations will redact exploitative details
